title: How personal agents choose what to buy
summary: Your next Black Friday customer may never see your product page. Personal agents like xAI’s Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, Instinct, and OpenAI’s Dots can compare offers across stores and recommend where to…
body_markdown:
Your next Black Friday customer may never see your product page. Personal agents like xAI’s Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, Instinct, and OpenAI’s Dots can compare offers across stores and recommend where to buy. In our tests, Grok Bot and Muse each recommended the bottle marked “In stock” over the same bottle at the same price marked “Only 3 left” in all 15 runs. Muse explained one recommendation as “same bottle and price, but less risk of it selling out before you order.” Scarcity sells to people, but it can send a shopping agent’s recommendation to another store.


At The Prompting Company, we study how AI assistants choose what to recommend and help teams make their products easier for agents to find and use. We simulated how a user would use these four agents to shop on live retail sites and on storefronts we built for the study. We tracked which offers they compared, what they recommended, and where they got stuck.


We used what we learned to build Benji, our own shopping agent, on Vercel’s open-source eve framework. We then tested Benji on the same storefronts to see how it compared offers and how far it got toward checkout.


## How we ran the study


Our broader personal-agent study ran from October 22 to November 12, 2026, and included 11,200 completed runs across 1,255 prompts. For this article, we revisited three shopping tests from that study covering bundle pricing, stock labels, and shipping fees. We looked at how Grok Bot, Muse, Instinct, and Dots handled those tests, then ran the same prompts with Benji. See the


[full study and methodology](https://promptingcompany.com/research/how-personal-agents-choose) .


For the stock test we built two test storefronts, Corvane and Tallowfin, as Next.js apps on Vercel. Both listed the same 24-ounce bottle for $34 with identical shipping and return terms. Only the stock label differed, and we swapped which storefront displayed “Only 3 left” between runs.


We counted a pick when an agent recommended or chose a single option by name. If it named no single choice, we recorded no pick. To count what drove each pick, we tagged up to three reasons the agent gave in its answer. For example, “price drove 57% of Muse’s picks” means Muse cited price as a reason in 57% of its picks.


We ran the same three shopping tests 15 times each with Benji, and tested it on five separate checkout tasks on live retail sites. Each run started in a fresh conversation in a browser hosted by Browserbase.


## What the shopping tests revealed


We tested how the four agents compared offers when pack size, stock labels, or shipping fees differed. We then gave Benji the same prompts and tracked what each agent recommended, what it could verify, and how far it got toward checkout.


### Benji picked the lower unit price


On Nécessaire’s store, one lip balm cost $28 and a two-pack cost $50. Grok Bot, Muse, and Instinct each recommended the two-pack in all 15 runs. Dots recommended it in 11 of 15. Benji also picked the bundle, at $25 per tube, in all 15 of its runs.


> *“It’s $50 for two 15 ml Mint balms, versus $28 for one: $25 per tube instead of $28, saving $6 compared with buying two singles.”*
>
>
> — Instinct

### Benji used the stock label to break a tie


On our test storefront, both Corvane and Tallowfin offered the same $34 bottle, and both were available to buy. Benji recognized that “Only 3 left” still meant the bottle was available. Since the two offers matched on product and price, it used the stock label to break the tie and chose “In stock” in all 15 runs. Grok Bot, Muse, and Dots did the same. Instinct picked “In stock” in 11 of 15 runs, picked “Only 3 left” in 2, and called it a tie in 2.


> *“Tallowfin is less likely to sell out before your order goes through.”*
>
>
> — Grok Bot

### Benji picked the retailer with the lowest delivered price


A brand’s site charged $52 for the lotion plus $8 for shipping. Other retailers offered the same lotion for $52 with free shipping. Benji picked a free-shipping retailer at $52 delivered in 14 of 15 runs. Muse and Dots also often picked a free-shipping retailer, while Grok Bot and Instinct mostly recommended the brand’s site.


> *“Buy it from Sephora, not direct: same bottle, but you save the shipping.”*
>
>
> — Muse

## How each agent shops


We built Benji around what we learned from watching four agents shop. Grok Bot tended to favor major retailers, Muse looked for the lowest price, Instinct often chose the brand’s own store, and Dots leaned on reviews. Those findings informed how Benji compares offers. It checks whether the item is available, compares unit prices, and flags shipping or tax it can’t verify.


Agent


What it prioritizes


What to watch for


What retailers can do


Grok Bot


Major retailers. It cited Amazon in 17.5% of runs, compared with 1.6% or less for the other agents.


It recommended the brand’s store in 8 of 15 runs, even though other retailers offered the same item at the same price with free shipping.


Make your products easy to find on major retailers and keep prices competitive.


Muse


Price. It cited price in 57% of its picks, the highest share among the agents tested.


When asked to choose between two options, Muse gave an “it depends” answer in 10 of 15 direct comparisons.


Show the unit price and shipping costs up front.


Instinct


The brand’s own store. It linked to the brand in 75% of answers. In 45%, that was the only link.


Often links only to the brand’s own site, with no store to compare.


Make stock status and return terms easy to find on your product pages.


Dots


Reviews. Reviews were cited in 41% of its picks, compared with 16% for price.


It reached the guest checkout form in 4 of 15 runs.


Make reviews easy to find and test whether Dots can reach guest checkout.


Benji


Delivered price. It uses a calculator to compare costs across sellers.


It paused to ask about a product option in one of five checkout tasks.


Show shipping costs, stock status, and product options on the page.


Grok Bot, Muse, Instinct, and Dots figures are from the study, October 22 to November 12, 2026.


## How Benji works


A single shopping request can take dozens of browser actions over several minutes, from finding the right product to checking the final price at checkout. We needed the agent to survive interruptions and leave a record we could check, and eve handles both:


- **Recover interrupted runs.**


Eve saves progress as the workflow runs, so when a local restart interrupted a conversation, we were able to pick it back up with


` --resume`


.


- **Verify what happened.**


The run log records each tool call and its result, so we can check what the agent actually did at each step.


## What happens in one Benji run


We asked Benji to find a 2-meter USB-C cable at Best Buy for under $25 and stop at the payment page. It got there in seven minutes.


- **Start.**


The request opens a conversation, and Benji loads its shopping rules.


- **Search.**


A web search finds 2-meter cables on Best Buy before any browser opens.


- **Browse.**


Benji acts on the page, reads it back, and repeats: it sets the ZIP code, sorts by price and opens the cheapest exact 2-meter cable.


- **Cart.**


It adds the cable, then reads the cart back to confirm the item and the $12.49 price.


- **Checkout.**


It checks out as a guest with the name and address from the request.


- **Stop.**


Best Buy shows a final total, which is the payment page, so Benji stops.


- **Price check.**


A calculator adds $12.49, free shipping, and $1.08 tax to get $13.57, under the $25 budget.


Benji pauses in three places. It stops at every payment page, asks when it needs input from the shopper, and hands the browser to a person at a sign-in page or a CAPTCHA.


## What broke when we deployed Benji


Eve runs each conversation as a durable workflow. A durable workflow saves its state after every step, one model call or one tool call, so a conversation can pause for the shopper and resume after a crash or a deploy.


We built Benji as if all 50 steps of a checkout would run on one machine. When we tested on Vercel, the first browser step failed. Each step can run in its own function, so files one step wrote to local disk were missing in the next.


The first fix was to package the browser’s files into every function. One file still lived on local disk: Benji’s list of saved store logins. A login saved in one step could be missing in the next, so some steps found an empty list. We moved the list to Vercel Blob, where every step reads the same copy.


## How Benji compares prices


Benji never adds up prices in the model. It passes the prices it saw to a calculator tool,


` compare_offers`


, which ranks only offers whose shipping and tax are both known. An offer with an unknown cost stays in the result but cannot be called the cheapest.


The tool sorts each incomplete offer into one of two groups. If its known costs already exceed the cheapest complete offer, it is out, because shipping only adds cost. Otherwise it is undecided, and Benji reports what is missing and tries to find it, for example by entering the shopper’s postcode in the cart.


```text
// Rank only offers whose shipping and tax are both known
const complete = priced
.filter((offer) => offer.unknownCosts.length === 0)
.sort((a, b) => a.knownSubtotal - b.knownSubtotal);
const lowest = complete.at(0);


const results = priced.map((offer) => {
const isComplete = offer.unknownCosts.length === 0;
return {
deliveredTotal: isComplete ? offer.knownSubtotal : null,
deliveredRank: isComplete ? complete.indexOf(offer) + 1 : null,
// Shipping only adds cost, so an offer whose known part is already
// above the cheapest complete offer cannot win
cannotBeLowest:
!isComplete &&
lowest !== undefined &&
offer.knownSubtotal > lowest.knownSubtotal,
};
});


// Offers that could still win once the missing cost is known
const undecided = results.filter(
(r) => r.deliveredTotal === null && !r.cannotBeLowest,
);
```


From server/offer-comparison.ts with input parsing and per-unit math left out.


## Final thoughts


A shopping agent can rule out an offer before the shopper ever sees it. Clear stock labels, unit prices, and shipping costs give agents what they need to compare offers fairly. Next, we plan to test the handoff at checkout: when a shopper takes over, does the cart still hold the right item and quantity, at the total the agent quoted?


> *“When you ask a personal agent to buy something, you’re letting it decide which stores to visit, which products to compare, and ultimately, where to spend your money. For retailers, that changes everything. Having the right product at the right price is no longer enough. Agents need to be able to find your products, understand what you’re offering, and make it all the way through checkout. As personal agents account for a growing share of shopping transactions, getting this right won’t just be an advantage. It’ll determine whether you can compete in this new agent economy.”*
>
>
> — Kevin Chandra, Co-founder, The Prompting Company


## What to check on your storefront


- **Show the total price with shipping.**


Make shipping costs and any free-shipping threshold easy to find. When the brand’s own store charged $8 for shipping, Muse picked a free-shipping retailer in 13 of 15 runs, Dots in 12 of 15, and Benji in 14 of 15 runs.


- **Price bundles to compete per unit.**


Give shoppers a lower unit price when they buy the bundle, and show the pack size, total price, and unit price together. Grok Bot, Muse, and Instinct each picked the lower-cost-per-tube bundle in all 15 runs. Dots picked it in 11 of 15, and Benji picked it in all 15 of its runs.


- **Lead with availability, not scarcity.**


Make it clear whether an item is available to buy, and show the remaining quantity as a secondary detail. When two otherwise identical offers were labeled “In stock” and “Only 3 left,” Grok Bot, Muse, Dots, and Benji each picked “In stock” in all 15 runs for that prompt.


- **Check that your bot protection lets shopping agents through.**


In our live test, one major retailer blocked Dots so it could not read the price or stock. On your own store, check whether the shopping agents you want to support can open a product page and add an item to the cart. If you host on Vercel, review your bot management settings for product and cart pages.


If you’re building a Shopify storefront, Vercel Shop is an open-source Next.js template that makes prices, availability, and product options readable by agents. To see how Grok Bot, Muse, Instinct, and Dots handle your storefront, try


[Retail Bench](https://promptingcompany.com/retail-benchmarks) .


## Track how personal agents shop for your product


We built personal agents into The Prompting Company from this research. Grok Bot and Muse ask your prompts in their own browsers, and TPC shows which product their answers land on.


[Read the launch post](https://promptingcompany.com/blog/personal-agents) .
